generatedProse.concept-context: Every field has referencing styles, and they differ in small but visible ways: where the year sits, whether titles are italicised, whether a citation is a name or a number. Your department will tell you which style to use, and once it is set the task is to apply it to every citation and reference without slips. A marker often turns to your reference list first, because a full and consistent list shows at a glance how widely and carefully you have read.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students hand in their work, each with a reference list.

Student A has read widely, but the reference list mixes styles. Some entries give the year in brackets and others do not; some titles are in italics and others in quotation marks; one citation uses a number. The marker cannot tell at a glance how carefully the sources were handled, and the inconsistency undercuts otherwise good research.

Student B has read the same sources and used one style throughout. Every citation matches a full reference, every reference follows the same pattern, and the list is alphabetical. The marker sees the scope of the reading at once, and the consistency reads as care and competence.

Both students did the reading. Only Student B's reference list let the marker see it.
generatedProse.summary: A referencing style is a set of rules for laying out citations and references, and every field has one it prefers. What matters most is consistency: one style, applied to every citation and reference without slips. Done well, your reference list shows a marker the scope and care of your research, and earns marks against the criteria. You can now cite, reference and apply a style with purpose in any subject you study.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Student B's reference list work in their favour with the marker?

items.text: One consistent style let the marker see the scope of the reading at a glance.
It listed more sources than Student A's did.
It used an unusual style that stood out.
It placed the references at the start of the work.

feedback.correct: That's right. A single consistent style let the marker take in the scope of the reading at once.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Both students read the same sources, so what made the difference?
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's list worked because one consistent style let the marker see the scope of the reading at a glance.
